doc.title: Jake Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997

title: Benny Goodman trios and playing without a bass
summary: Hanna admires Goodman's trio recordings and describes playing piano-drums trios with Peplowski, Varro, Sutton, Bunch and McKenna.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: B.G., yeah. Yeah, he was great, great. He never cared for me, but gez, I heard some fantastic things he’s done. Still, even now, you’ll bring back some old things he did. My wife and I were listening to him on a tape, 1935, 1938 with Gene and Teddy. They had to divide it up and it was much better as a trio, it really was. They could do whatever they wanted you know? They didn’t have to worry about getting the keys right in the middle of a song, just look at Teddy and Teddy looked at him and they knew just what they were doing. We’re trying the same thing with Kenny Peplowski and Johnny Varro and myself. We rarely get together but when we do it’s very exciting, very exciting. They’re great. The guys are great.
How does it change your playing to work without a bass player?

Well you adjust the playing. Sometimes I just leave the hi hat off. And you play off the snare and the bass drum stays very steady. You’ve got to re-tune it where it gets a nice tone. And it all depends on that piano player see? You’ve got to have a nice, loose left

hand. Can’t be pounding. Teddy can play you know. There’s only one Teddy Wilson. And that’s Johnny Varro. But Johnny is very good, absolutely. And Ralph Sutton. We have a good, easy time with Ralph and we have an easy time with John Bunch, and Dave McKenna, he’s born for that, Dave McKenna is the king of that stuff. In fact he doesn’t need us. So the hell with Dave.
